subcategory: Gulf Coast native bog spider lily bulb

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in consistently damp, humus-rich soil in sun to part sun; this Florida panhandle endemic favors boggy conditions similar to those preferred by pitcher plants.

directions: Traub's spider lily is a small, slowly stoloniferous species endemic to wet, boggy habitats of the Florida panhandle, forming low rosettes of narrow, grass-like green foliage that spread gradually to form loose patches without becoming aggressive. In late spring each rosette sends up a foot-tall scape topped with two or three narrow-petaled, pure white, sweetly fragrant flowers typical of the genus's spidery form. Because it comes from constantly moist, low-nutrient boggy ground, it performs best where soil stays damp year-round, such as pond margins, rain gardens, or bog plantings alongside pitcher plants, rather than in average garden beds. Plants go winter dormant and resent being allowed to dry out completely during the growing season.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-6 inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in part sun to light shade; unlike most spider lilies this Mexican species prefers shade and resents full-sun exposure.

directions: Native to Mexico and once thought extinct before being rediscovered, eucharis-leaf spider lily is distinguished from most of its genus by its broad, glossy, eucharis-like basal leaves rather than the strap-shaped foliage typical of hymenocallis. In midsummer it sends up foot-tall flower spikes carrying two or three upright, star-shaped white blooms per stem. It multiplies quickly into dense, fast-spreading clumps under the right conditions and is unusual among spider lilies in preferring light shade to part sun rather than full sun, making it a good choice for a shaded border where sun-loving hymenocallis would struggle. Foliage dies back in winter and resprouts reliably once soil warms in spring.

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in rich, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to part sun; tolerates clay, sand, and occasional standing water.

directions: 'Carnival' is a Thad Howard hybrid crinum, a cross of Crinum bulbispermum with his own earlier hybrid 'Thaddeus Howard', bred for an especially full, symmetrical flower head. In midsummer it sends up roughly three-foot scapes topped with ten to thirteen large, fragrant, rich pink blooms edged and striped with pale white, all opening together for a dramatic, uniform burst rather than the staggered bloom typical of many crinums. The glossy apple-green foliage forms a broad mound three to four feet across and persists as semi-evergreen in milder winters, going fully deciduous after hard freezes further north. Like other Gulf South heirloom crinums, it is extremely tough once established, tolerating heavy clay, wet soil, and summer heat, and slowly produces offset bulbs that can be divided every few years to expand the planting.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; an old, reliably reblooming apomictic hybrid that comes true from seed since all seedlings are clones of the parent.

directions: 'Sunset' is a long-grown, apomictic rain lily hybrid, meaning that because its seed is produced clonally, seedlings reliably reproduce the parent's peachy-pink flowers rather than segregating into variable colors the way sexually produced rain lily seed often does. Silver-dollar-sized blooms open in a warm peach-pink shade with a darker rosy blush along the outside of each petal, carried on ten-inch stalks above flat, grassy green foliage. Flowering begins in early summer and continues in flushes through the season, with the heaviest flush appearing two to three days after a rain event or deep watering. It is a tough, low-maintenance bulb, equally happy in full sun or light afternoon shade, and increases steadily into dense flowering clumps with minimal care.

planting.note: Plant bulbs about 4 inches deep in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; a compact species best protected from winter wet in cooler zones.

directions: Dwarf pink rain lily is a diminutive Mexican species that packs surprisingly large, nearly three-inch, funnel-shaped bright pink flowers onto a plant barely taller than its own foliage. Glossy, narrow, linear leaves stay low and grassy, with the big trumpet blooms appearing in late summer and early autumn, triggered by seasonal rainfall as in other rain lilies. It prefers sharply drained soil over chalk, loam, or sand and full sun, and resents cold, wet winters, so in anything short of mild coastal zones it is best grown where winter drainage is excellent or lifted and stored like a tender bulb. Takes a few years from a small offset to reach full flowering size, after which it multiplies steadily.

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above soil level in well-drained soil with afternoon shade; sited where summer foliage of companion plants can hide the leafless bloom stalks.

directions: Hayward's surprise lily arose from a 1948 shipment of Chinese bulbs received by Florida bulb grower Wyndham Hayward and was later described as a hybrid of Lycoris sprengeri and Lycoris radiata var. pumila; it was formally named for him in 1957. Like other surprise lilies it blooms leafless in late summer, sending up bare eighteen-to-twenty-four-inch stalks topped with clusters of bright magenta-pink flowers whose petal tips carry a distinctive blue cast inherited from its sprengeri parent. Strap-like foliage emerges separately in fall or winter after bloom, persists through the cooler months, and dies back by late spring well before flowering, so it is best paired with later-emerging perennials that can mask the bare scapes. Because of its radiata pumila parentage it is somewhat less cold-hardy and more winter-active than many other garden lycoris, so it suits the milder end of its hardiness range best.
